section.title: Judgment and Final Hope
section.sectionRationale: Isaiah's last chapter closes the book the way it opened, with a courtroom scene, but now the horizon has stretched to its farthest point: heaven as God's throne, a nation born in a single day, God's people nursed like infants at Jerusalem's comfort, and a terrible final image of unquenchable fire and an undying worm for those who rebel. It is the last word of a book that has moved from Judah's sin to the new heavens and new earth.
section.thesis: The God whose throne is heaven and footstool is earth esteems the humble and contrite, will comfort His people like a mother comforts her child and gather every nation to see His glory, while those who persist in rebellion face a judgment whose fire is never quenched and whose worm never dies.
section.frameNote: Four movements: heaven My throne, earth My footstool, the humble and contrite esteemed; Zion gives birth suddenly, before she was in labor; as a mother comforts, so I will comfort you; and the LORD comes in fire, gathering the nations, closing on the sober warning of unquenched fire.

units.label: Heaven is My throne, earth is My footstool

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me? Or where will My place of repose be?
Has not My hand made all these things? And so they came into being,” declares the LORD. “This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and {{nakeh|contrite}} in spirit, who trembles at My word.

Whoever slaughters an ox is like one who slays a man; whoever sacrifices a lamb is like one who breaks a dog’s neck; whoever presents a grain offering is like one who offers pig’s blood; whoever offers frankincense is like one who blesses an idol. Indeed, they have chosen their own ways and delighted in their abominations.

So I will choose their punishment and I will bring terror upon them, because I called and no one answered, I spoke and no one listened. But they did evil in My sight and chose that in which I did not delight.”

You who tremble at His word, hear the word of the LORD: “Your brothers who hate you and exclude you because of My name have said, ‘Let the LORD be glorified that we may see your joy!’ But they will be put to shame.”
Hear the uproar from the city; listen to the voice from the temple! It is the voice of the LORD, repaying His enemies what they deserve!

units.label: Before she was in labor, she gave birth
units.note: a nation born in a day

verses.text: “Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before she was in pain, she delivered a boy.
Who has heard of such as this? Who has seen such things? Can a country be born in a day or a nation be delivered in an instant? Yet as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children.
Shall I bring a baby to the point of birth and not deliver it?” says the LORD. “Or will I who deliver close the womb?” says your God.

units.label: As a mother comforts, so I will comfort you

verses.text: Be glad for Jerusalem and rejoice over her, all who love her. Rejoice greatly with her, all who mourn over her,
so that you may nurse and be satisfied at her comforting breasts; you may drink deeply and delight yourselves in her glorious abundance.
For this is what the LORD says: “I will extend peace to her like a river, and the wealth of nations like a flowing stream; you will nurse and be carried on her arm, and bounced upon her knees.
As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you, and you will be consoled over Jerusalem.”
When you see, you will rejoice, and you will flourish like grass; then the hand of the LORD will be revealed to His servants, but His wrath will be shown to His enemies.

units.label: The LORD will come with fire
units.note: gathering all nations to see My glory

verses.text: For behold, the LORD will come with fire, His chariots are like a whirlwind, to execute His anger with fury and His rebuke with flames of fire.
For by fire and by His sword, the LORD will execute judgment on all flesh, and many will be slain by the LORD.
“Those who consecrate and purify themselves to enter the groves, to follow one in the center of those who eat the flesh of swine and vermin and rats, will perish together,” declares the LORD.
“And I, knowing their deeds and thoughts, am coming to gather all nations and tongues, and they will come and see My glory.

I will establish a sign among them, and I will send survivors from among them to the nations, to Tarshish, Put, and the archers of Lud; to Tubal, Javan, and the islands far away who have not heard of My fame or seen My glory. So they will proclaim My glory among the nations.

And they will bring all your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the LORD on horses and chariots and wagons, on mules and camels, to My holy mountain Jerusalem,” says the LORD, “just as the Israelites bring an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD.”
“And I will select some of them as priests and Levites,” says the LORD.
“For just as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, will endure before Me,” declares the LORD, “so your descendants and your name will endure.
From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me,” says the LORD.

“As they go forth, they will see the corpses of the men who have rebelled against Me; for their {{tola|worm}} will never die, their fire will never be quenched, and they will be a horror to all mankind.”

nakeh.gloss: Contrite in spirit, crushed low. God says He esteems this one above every temple or sacrifice, echoing the same promise of 57:15, and anticipating Jesus' beatitude, blessed are the poor in spirit, Matthew 5:3; true worship is finally a matter of the heart's posture, not the size or splendor of any house built for God.

tola.gloss: Worm, maggot, associated with decay of corpses left unburied, a picture of shameful, ongoing ruin. Jesus quotes this closing verse three times, unchanged, to describe hell, where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched, Mark 9:44-48, taking Isaiah's final, sobering image as His own description of final judgment.

basic.context: Isaiah's last chapter returns to a courtroom scene, God's true worship is not a temple but a humble, trembling heart, and moves through a startling image, a nation born in a single day, to tender comfort, God nursing His people like a mother, before ending with a picture of gathered nations and a final warning of unquenched fire for the unrepentant.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter refuses a tidy, uniformly comforting ending. It holds together God's global gathering of the nations to see His glory and a final, sobering image of judgment that Jesus Himself later quotes of hell. Both are equally serious and equally real; neither should be softened to make the book end more comfortably than its own words allow.
basic.originalLanguages: God esteems the one who is humble and nakeh ruach, contrite in spirit, more than any temple built for Him. And the closing image of tola'ah, worm, that never dies, alongside unquenched fire, is quoted three times unchanged by Jesus in Mark 9 as His own description of final judgment.
basic.typology: Heaven as God's throne and earth as His footstool is quoted by Stephen and echoed by Jesus of true worship transcending any building. The nation born in a day anticipates the sudden, miraculous birth of the church at Pentecost. God comforting His people as a mother comforts a child anticipates Jesus' own tender, maternal image of longing to gather Jerusalem's children.
basic.christ: Stephen quotes verse 1 directly before his martyrdom, heaven is My throne and earth is My footstool, arguing that no house made with hands can contain God, Acts 7:49. Jesus quotes the final verse of this chapter three times unchanged, Mark 9:44-48, to describe hell, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched, taking Isaiah's last, sober image as His own words about eternal judgment.
basic.god: God is both universally worshiped, gathering every nation and tongue to see His glory, and terrifyingly just, His fire unquenched for those who rebel against Him; He is also as tender as a nursing mother toward His own people, holding infinite majesty and infinite gentleness together without contradiction.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 7:49 quotes verse 1 of God's transcendence over any physical temple. Mark 9:44-48 quotes verse 24 three times unchanged, of the unquenched fire and undying worm of hell. Revelation 21:1 and 22 fulfill the new heavens and new earth named again in verse 22.
basic.oneStory: The book that opened accusing a rebellious nation closes gathering every nation to see God's glory, comforting His people like a nursing mother, and warning, in words Jesus Himself later takes up, that rebellion against God ends in a fire that is never quenched. Isaiah's last word is both the widest possible hope and the most sober possible warning, both fulfilled in Christ.

context.literary:
The last chapter of Isaiah is a bookend. The book opened with 'Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth,' Isaiah 1:2, calling the created order to witness a family quarrel. It closes with heaven as God's throne and earth as His footstool, 66:1. The opening chapter attacked sacrifices offered by people whose hands were full of blood, 1:11 to 17, and 66:3 returns to the same charge. Isaiah 1:29 shamed those who delighted in sacred gardens and 66:17 condemns those who consecrate themselves to enter the groves. Isaiah 1:31 ended with a fire that no one could quench, and 66:24 ends with a fire that will never be quenched. The prophet has brought his hearers round a long circle and left them at the same door with the stakes raised.

Within the chapter there are four movements. Verses 1 to 6 ask what kind of house God wants, and set the humble who tremble against those who choose their own way. Verses 7 to 14 turn to birth and nursing, with Zion as mother and the LORD as the one who delivers. Verses 15 to 17 bring the LORD in fire and sword to judge. Verses 18 to 24 gather the nations, send survivors out as missionaries, make priests of some, and end with an enduring new creation and a sight outside the city.

Two threads bind the chapter. One is the word 'all flesh,' kol basar, which has run through the book since 40:5, 'all humanity together will see it.' It reappears at 66:16, 23 and 24 and is the unit of both the final worship and the final judgment. The other is the pairing of the same two groups in one verse after another, those who tremble and those who do not, servants and enemies, the comforted and the repaid.

The ending is hard on purpose. Jewish practice in reading Isaiah, Malachi, Lamentations and Ecclesiastes aloud is to repeat the verse before the final one when the last verse is a sad one, so that the reading ends on 'from one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me,' 66:23. The practice shows how heavy the last verse has always felt, and also shows that readers did not want to delete it.
context.historical:
The first hearers of the chapter were people who had already built a second temple. It was finished in the sixth year of Darius, Ezra 6:15, after the push led by Haggai, who said, 'build the house, so that I may take pleasure in it and be glorified,' Haggai 1:8. So 66:1, 'What kind of house will you build for Me?' cannot be a rejection of the temple. It reads better as a warning to people who treated the building as a guarantee, the same attitude Jeremiah had met when the crowds chanted 'This is the temple of the LORD,' Jeremiah 7:4. A building can express worship. It cannot contain the one who made the heavens.

The chapter also shows a community in conflict. In verse 5 the faithful, 'you who tremble at His word,' are hated and excluded by their own kin, who sneer, 'Let the LORD be glorified that we may see your joy!' The scorn is religious: the persecutors speak the language of piety and use it against the humble. Ezra 9:4 and 10:3 call those who gathered around the word of God by the same word, those who tremble, and the title seems to name a recognisable party of the devout.

The sacrifices in verse 3 are drawn from the daily vocabulary of the cult, the ox, the lamb, the grain offering and frankincense, set beside things that the law forbids or treats as unclean, a man struck down, a dog's neck broken, pig's blood, an idol. The mention of a neck being broken recalls the law of the firstborn donkey, Exodus 13:13, and of the heifer in the valley, Deuteronomy 21:4. Verse 17 pushes it to pigs, vermin and rats eaten in groves, a picture of a cult at the edge of the law.

The list of places in verse 19 reads like a map of the known world: Tarshish in the far west, Put and Lud, Tubal and Javan, and 'the islands far away.' These names come from the table of nations in Genesis 10:2, 4, 6 and 13, so the prophet is naming the descendants of Noah's sons. The brothers brought on 'horses and chariots and wagons, on mules and camels' are exiles and Gentiles being carried in procession to the holy mountain. The final scene, in which the worshippers 'go forth' and see the corpses, places the picture of judgment outside the city, close to the setting Jeremiah had used for the valley where children were once burned, Jeremiah 7:31 to 33.
context.canonical:
This chapter is one of the most used in the whole of the New Testament for the two truths with which it closes. Stephen quotes verses 1 and 2 in the speech that ends in his death, Acts 7:48 to 50, and Paul uses the same idea on the Areopagus when he says that God 'does not live in temples made by human hands,' Acts 17:24. Jesus' words, 'something greater than the temple is here,' Matthew 12:6, belong to the same development, and Paul tells believers that they are God's temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

The birth imagery of verses 7 to 9 and the consolation of verses 10 to 13 are taken up by Paul and John. Paul uses the image of the 'Jerusalem above' as our mother, Galatians 4:26, quoting Isaiah 54:1, and Jesus compares the pain of the disciples to a woman's labour that turns to joy, John 16:21. The woman of Revelation 12:5 gives birth to a son who rules the nations. The gathering of the nations and the priests of verses 18 to 21 are applied to the mission of the apostles. Paul describes his work as a priestly service so that 'the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God,' Romans 15:16, language that is very close to 66:20, and Revelation says that the redeemed have been made 'a kingdom and priests,' Revelation 5:10.

The last verse is picked up in the Gospels and beyond. Jesus quotes it on the lips of the Lord of the final judgment in Mark 9:48, 'where their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched,' and Daniel 12:2 uses the same word of everlasting contempt for the wicked who rise. Revelation shows the new heaven and the new earth, 21:1, and a city to which the nations bring their glory, with the unclean kept outside, 21:24 to 27, so that the same two scenes stand side by side.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet's last word was meant to settle a question that every hearer in the book's final section carried: who actually belongs to God? His answer is surprising. It is not those with the right building, the right ancestry or the right sacrifice, but 'he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word,' 66:2. The chapter wanted the humble, who were being excluded, to know that God sees them and will vindicate them in public, and it wanted the confident, who were doing the excluding, to know that He sees them too.

He also meant to enlarge the hearers' sense of what God is doing. The birth of a nation in a day, the comfort that outlasts the long grief of the exile and the gathering of 'all nations and tongues' were meant to stretch a small, struggling community to see that its story belongs to a world-wide purpose. They are not simply to be restored. They are to be a source of mission, since survivors are sent to the farthest places to declare God's glory.

And he meant the book to end with a warning that could not be missed. A book that had offered comfort in chapter 40 and glory in chapter 60 closes with a sight of the dead who rebelled, because hope that does not recognise a real alternative is sentiment. The intended effect is reverence, a trembling at God's word that is also the mark of those He esteems.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of the chapter is description of what God will do, and some of it uses the categories of Israel's worship that belong to its own time. The picture that all mankind will come to worship 'from one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another,' 66:23, uses the calendar of the temple to describe unbroken worship. It does not mean that Christians must keep the New Moon festival. Paul says that these are 'a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:16 and 17. The point is the regularity and universality of worship, not its calendar.

The comparisons in verse 3 are not a rejection of sacrifice as such, which the law commanded. They describe what happens when offerings are made by people who live in abomination, so the ritual becomes an insult. The practical lesson for believers is the same as the one in 1 Samuel 15:22 and Micah 6:6 to 8: obedience and humility come before the ritual and are the test of it.

The image of God comforting 'as a mother comforts her son' is a metaphor about tenderness. Scripture does not change God's self-revelation as Father by it, any more than it does in Isaiah 42:14 or 49:15. It adds to our picture of God's care without overturning the names He gives Himself.

The last verse is a description of a scene and also the text Jesus quoted in a warning. Where Jesus uses it, in Mark 9:43 to 48, it is attached to a command: deal ruthlessly with whatever causes you to sin. The passage is not given so that readers can speculate about the details of judgment but so that they can take seriously what is at stake in how they live and respond to God.

debates.question: What does the image of the undying worm and unquenched fire in verse 24 teach about the fate of the lost?

views.label: Unending conscious punishment
views.case: Jesus quotes the verse in Mark 9:48 as a description of hell, and sets the 'eternal punishment' of the lost beside 'eternal life' in Matthew 25:46. Revelation 14:11 speaks of smoke rising forever and Revelation 20:10 of torment day and night. On this reading the Isaiah image, which describes corpses, is taken up by Jesus and given a wider meaning.

views.label: Final destruction, the fire consumes completely
views.case: In Isaiah the worm and the fire are working on corpses, and the point is that nothing will stop them until the work is done. Elsewhere an 'unquenchable' fire is one that cannot be put out and consumes what it burns, Jeremiah 17:27 and Ezekiel 20:47 and 48. This reading points to texts about destruction such as Matthew 10:28 and 2 Thessalonians 1:9, and holds that the language stresses finality and not endless experience.

views.label: Figurative, a picture of shame and finality
views.case: The setting recalls the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, Jeremiah 7:31 to 33, and the scene is of bodies left unburied, the deepest shame in the ancient world. The Hebrew word that closes the verse is the word of horror or abhorrence, and Daniel 12:2 uses it for 'everlasting contempt.' On this view the images do not set out a mechanism but declare that rebellion ends in a judgment that is public, permanent and shameful.

debates.bearing: All three views take the passage as a warning of a real, serious and final judgment, and Jesus' own use is a warning, not a lecture. A reader should hold the common core firmly and be careful not to claim more precision about the manner than the text gives.

debates.question: Who are the priests and Levites of verse 21?

views.label: Gentiles drawn from the nations
views.case: The verse says 'I will select some of them,' and the nearest 'them' in the passage are the nations brought in verses 19 and 20. Isaiah 56:6 and 7 had already welcomed foreigners who minister to the LORD. On this reading the verse is a radical opening of the priesthood beyond Israel, which the New Testament takes up in Revelation 5:10 and 1 Peter 2:9.

views.label: Jewish exiles brought back from the nations
views.case: The 'brothers' brought from all the nations in verse 20 are Israelites, and the priests and Levites of verse 21 may be chosen from among those returned exiles. This fits the surrounding emphasis on the gathering of the dispersed, Isaiah 56:8, and the temple setting of the verse.

views.label: A picture of the whole redeemed people
views.case: Whoever is meant, the effect is to say that the people of the new age are all given access to God. Believers are called 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, and Revelation 1:6 says Christ 'has made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father.' The language of Levites is the only vocabulary the prophet had for full access.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew leaves the antecedent open, and the three readings are not rivals so much as stages. In every case the prophet is making the priesthood larger than its old boundaries, which is how the New Testament uses it.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for those who 'tremble' in verses 2 and 5 is a form of the root hared, an earnest, bodily reverence. It is the word used in Ezra 9:4 and 10:3 for those who gathered around the word and the command of God, and later Jewish usage took the plural, charedim, as a name for the devout. In Isaiah the trembling is directed at a word, not a building: God esteems the one who 'trembles at My word,' so that the sacred object of fear is what He has said.

Verse 3 is written in a clipped series of participles. The Hebrew sets the pairs side by side, 'the one slaughtering the ox, the one striking down a man,' with no word for 'like,' and translations supply the comparison. That is why interpreters differ over whether the verse says that the offering is as bad as murder or that these worshippers do both. The verb for the dog's neck, araf, is the verb used for breaking the neck of the firstborn donkey, Exodus 13:13, and the heifer, Deuteronomy 21:4, so the image is of a ritual act turned into something repulsive. The word at the end of the verse, aven, which the BSB renders 'idol,' carries the ideas of wickedness and nothingness. The same word is behind Beth-aven, the 'house of wickedness' that Hosea 4:15 uses as a nickname for Bethel.

The birth imagery in verse 9 answers a line from earlier in the book. When Hezekiah's envoys came to Isaiah in despair, they said that 'children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them,' Isaiah 37:3. The word for 'point of birth' there is related to the verb the LORD uses in 66:9, 'Shall I bring a baby to the point of birth and not deliver it?' It is a deliberate answer. What the king said was a complaint that God would not finish what He had begun, and the LORD says that He will not leave a birth half done.

The consolation of verse 13 uses the verb nacham, 'comfort.' It is the verb that opened the second half of the book, 'Comfort, comfort My people,' Isaiah 40:1, and it is used here as the last word of promise, with the subject a mother. The peace that comes 'like a river,' verse 12, echoes Isaiah 48:18, where obedience would have made peace like a river. Verse 14 says that 'your bones' will flourish like grass, a bodily phrase for new vigour, and the grass of 40:7 and 8, which withers, is set against it.

In verses 16, 23 and 24 the expression kol basar, 'all flesh,' appears. The BSB translates it as 'all flesh' in verse 16 and 'all mankind' in verses 23 and 24, but it is the phrase of Isaiah 40:5, 'all humanity together will see it.' In the first part of the book flesh is weak, like grass, and in the last it is summoned to see glory and to see the judgment.

The last word of the book, deraon, which the BSB renders as 'a horror,' appears elsewhere in the same sense in Daniel 12:2, 'shame and everlasting contempt.' The verb of the fire, 'will never be quenched,' is the verb of Isaiah 1:31, 'with no one to quench the flames,' so that the book ends on the same word with which it began its warning.

typology.fulfillment: God asks what house could contain Him and answers that He esteems the humble person. Stephen draws the consequence, 'the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands,' Acts 7:48. In Christ the answer takes flesh: Jesus calls His own body the temple, John 2:19 to 21, and says that 'something greater than the temple is here,' Matthew 12:6. Believers are then called a temple built together in Him, Ephesians 2:21 and 22, and the final city has no temple because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The type falls short because the Old Testament temple was a shadow that still pointed to a place, while the true dwelling is a person and a people.

typology.type: A nation born in a day, Isaiah 66:7-9
typology.fulfillment: Zion gives birth to children before she has labour pains, and the prophet asks, 'Can a country be born in a day?' Pentecost provides a pattern of such a day, when about three thousand were added to the believers at once, Acts 2:41, with Jews from every nation present, Acts 2:5 to 11. Paul speaks of 'the Jerusalem above' as the mother of the free, Galatians 4:26, and John describes a woman who bears a son who rules the nations, Revelation 12:5. The text does not name Pentecost, so the link is a pattern. The type falls short because Pentecost is a beginning, and the full birth of the people of God is not completed until the resurrection.

typology.type: The nations brought as an offering, Isaiah 66:19-21
typology.fulfillment: Survivors are sent to far places that have not heard of God's fame, and they bring the Gentiles to Jerusalem as an offering to the LORD. Paul takes his own work in these terms, as a priestly service 'so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit,' Romans 15:16. Jesus gives the commission to 'make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:19, and the vision ends with a multitude from every nation and tribe before the throne, Revelation 7:9. The escalation is that the offering is made holy by the Spirit and by Christ's work. The type falls short because Isaiah still sets his picture in a Jerusalem with a temple and animals, while the New Testament places the gathering around the Lamb.

The picture of all mankind worshipping at each New Moon and Sabbath uses the rhythm of the temple to say that worship will be continual and universal. The letter to the Hebrews says that 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9, and Paul calls the festivals and Sabbaths 'a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:17. The escalation is that the rest is entered through Christ and does not depend on a calendar. The type falls short because the shadow marked time, while the substance is the presence of the Lord who is the rest.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most directly through its opening question. 'What kind of house will you build for Me?' Stephen's answer, in Acts 7, is delivered to people who have just rejected Jesus, and it ends with a vision: 'I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,' Acts 7:56. The One who cannot be contained in a building is the One in whom the true dwelling of God has come, as John's Gospel says, 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. When the temple was destroyed, Jesus had already said that His body was the real temple, John 2:19 to 21, and He had told the crowd that 'something greater than the temple is here.'

The person whom God esteems is the person Jesus blesses. 'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,' Matthew 5:3. In the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, the man who beat his breast and said, 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!' went home justified, Luke 18:13 and 14. Isaiah 66:2 is the portrait of that man, and Jesus is both the one who recognises him and, as the Servant who listens to the Father's word and obeys, the model of that humility.

The mother's comfort is acted out in Jesus. He says over Jerusalem, 'how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!' Luke 13:34, and He weeps as He approaches the city, Luke 19:41. The Father of compassion and God of all comfort, 2 Corinthians 1:3 and 4, comforts through the Son. The two sides of the chapter, the comforting mother and the coming fire, belong to the same Jesus, who is the one who weeps over the city and also the one who says that the Father has given all judgment to Him, John 5:22.

The gathering of the nations takes shape in His promises. 'I have other sheep that are not of this fold,' John 10:16, and 'And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself,' John 12:32. God says in verse 18 that the nations 'will come and see My glory.' John says of Jesus, 'We have seen His glory,' John 1:14, and Jesus prays that His people will be where He is, 'that they may see the glory You gave Me,' John 17:24. The glory of the LORD that all flesh will see, Isaiah 40:5, is revealed in the face of the Son.

It is Jesus who gives the final verse its weight. In Mark 9:43 to 48 He says it of hell and uses it to press His hearers to deal with sin at any cost. The man who speaks most tenderly of the Father is the one who speaks most plainly of this. Luke 12:5 shows the same pairing: 'Fear the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear Him!' A reader who believes that Jesus is gentle has to include these words, and a reader who fears them has to remember who says them.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The passage does not name Jesus and is full of the images of its own day, temples, Levites and horses. The links above are those the New Testament itself draws, and what the chapter gives is the shape of the gospel: a God who dwells with the humble, a family born by His power, a people drawn from every nation and a warning that matches the invitation in its seriousness.
study.god:
The chapter opens with the greatest claim of the book about God's size, and follows it at once with His nearness. Heaven is His throne and earth is His footstool, and the hands that made everything are the hands that pick out one person, the one who is humble and trembles at His word. Isaiah 57:15 says the same in other words: the One 'who inhabits eternity' dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit.' A theology that keeps only the first half makes God remote, and one that keeps only the second makes Him small. The chapter makes the greatness the reason the nearness is wonderful.

God is shown as the judge of worship. He is not impressed by the ox or the lamb brought by people who have chosen their own ways, and He says, 'I called and no one answered, I spoke and no one listened,' verse 4. What He wants is obedience, a heart that listens. That is not a rejection of the cult He commanded. It is an insistence that the cult is the servant of the covenant. He also knows what is hidden. 'I, knowing their deeds and thoughts, am coming,' verse 18, and the footnote shows how compressed the phrase is. Nothing in the secret groves or the heart escapes Him.

The chapter is clear about His faithfulness to finish. 'Shall I bring a baby to the point of birth and not deliver it?' is a rhetorical question to which the only answer is no. What He starts, He completes. It is a promise that rests on His character, and it answers the sense of abandonment in the prayer of chapters 63 and 64. He is also tender, and the picture of Him as a mother who comforts is among the most intimate in the Old Testament. It sits next to His majesty without strain, as the same God.

He is the Lord of all nations. The gathering of 'all nations and tongues' shows that His glory is not the possession of one people. He sends survivors to places 'who have not heard of My fame or seen My glory,' so that His fame is something that must be declared, and He takes priests from among them. He is the Creator of a new heaven and a new earth that will 'endure before Me,' verse 22, which means that His promises have a permanence matched by the permanence of what He makes.

He is also a consuming fire, and the chapter does not hide it. The coming 'with fire' and 'chariots like a whirlwind,' verse 15, and the closing image, show a God whose holiness is a real danger to those who persist in rebellion. Hebrews says, 'Our God is a consuming fire,' Hebrews 12:29, in the same breath that it calls for reverence and awe. His anger is not a loss of control but the other face of His love for what is good. It is why He can be trusted with the final word about justice.

For worship, the chapter points toward trembling and joy together. It asks us to come with the humility of those He esteems, to take His word seriously, to rejoice with Jerusalem, and to carry His fame to those who have not heard it. It also asks us never to treat the nearness of God as something that makes His holiness safe.

crossReferences.note: Stephen quotes verses 1 and 2 to say that the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands. He uses Isaiah's question to expose a trust in the temple that had replaced obedience, just before he is stoned and sees Jesus standing at God's right hand.

The book's first chapter rejects sacrifices from people whose hands are covered with blood and calls them to learn to do right. Isaiah 66:3 repeats the charge in its last chapter, so that the book opens and closes with the same lesson about worship without obedience.

The One 'who inhabits eternity' dwells with the humble and contrite to revive them. It is the clearest earlier statement of what 66:2 says in one line, and it shows that God's majesty and God's nearness to the lowly are taught together across the section.

Hezekiah's officials say that children have come to the point of birth but there is no strength to deliver them. Isaiah 66:9 reverses the despair, as the LORD asks whether He will bring to birth and not deliver, and answers it with the birth of a nation in a day.

The second half of the book opens with 'Comfort, comfort My people' and the promise that all flesh will see God's glory revealed. Isaiah 66:13 and 18 to 23 return to both, and so the comfort of the beginning is finished and the seeing of glory is enlarged to all nations.

Paul calls the 'Jerusalem above' our mother and quotes Isaiah 54:1 about the barren woman who has more children than the married one. It is the New Testament's use of the same mother Zion that gives birth in Isaiah 66:7 to 9.

Jesus compares the pain of the disciples to a woman in labour whose anguish is forgotten in the joy of a child born into the world. It uses the same birth picture that Isaiah applies to Zion, and shows the pattern of sorrow turning to joy in the death and resurrection.

Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks, but they were unwilling. It is a maternal picture of His love, alongside the comfort of Isaiah 66:13, and it shows the tender and the sorrowful aspects held together.

Jesus tells His hearers to cut off whatever causes them to sin rather than be thrown into hell, 'where their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.' The last line comes from Isaiah 66:24 and shows that He took the prophet's closing sight as a real warning.

Some who rise from the dust will wake to 'shame and everlasting contempt.' The final word uses the same term as the 'horror' of Isaiah 66:24, so that the two prophets share a vocabulary for the lasting shame of those who rebelled against God.

The valley of Hinnom is where children were burned, and God says it will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, with corpses left for the birds. The picture of unburied bodies outside the city lies behind the scene of Isaiah 66:24.

Paul describes his ministry as a priestly service so that the Gentiles might become an offering acceptable to God. It closely matches Isaiah 66:20, in which the nations are brought as an offering, and many readers see Paul as understanding his mission in these terms.

On the day of Pentecost, Jews from every nation under heaven hear the wonders of God in their own languages. It shows the nations gathered in Jerusalem at the moment the church is born, a first fruit of the gathering of verse 18 and a reversal of the scattering at Babel.

There is no temple in the new Jerusalem, the nations walk by its light and bring in their glory, the gates are never shut, and nothing unclean enters. It gathers the temple question of 66:1, the nations of 66:18 and the separation of 66:24 into one scene.

Believers receive an unshakable kingdom and are told to worship with reverence and awe, 'for our God is a consuming fire.' It joins the invitation and the warning in the same way the last chapter of Isaiah does, and it puts the fire of verse 15 in the context of worship.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 66 is the end of a book and a window onto the end of the Bible. The Bible begins with heaven and earth made by God's hand and with a garden in which He walked with people. It follows the story of how people were driven out, scattered at Babel into the nations of Genesis 10 and 11, and called back by a promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Isaiah 66 takes each of these threads and ties it off. Heaven and earth are called as witnesses at the start of the book, and now they are God's throne and footstool. The scattered nations are gathered from Tarshish to the farthest islands. The family that Genesis called out is made a source of blessing, with survivors sent to proclaim God's glory.

The chapter is also the last word of the Old Testament on the question of worship. From the garden to the tabernacle to the temple, the story is one of a God who wants to live with His people and who gives them a place for it. But Isaiah asks what kind of house could contain Him and answers with a person, not a building: the humble one who trembles at His word. That prepares the New Testament's claim that Christ is the temple and His people are being built into one, John 2:21 and Ephesians 2:22, until the city appears with no temple in it because God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22.

The story also moves through division. Isaiah 66 splits humanity into those who tremble and those who do not, and it does so without sentimentality. The comfort given to the first group and the fire kept for the second are both final. The Bible's last chapters keep the same pattern, with those who wash their robes entering the city and the unclean outside, Revelation 22:14 and 15. The warning that Jesus attaches to the closing verse is the reason the invitation is urgent. Nothing in the story allows a reader to treat the gospel as optional.

The new creation is the horizon. 'Just as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, will endure before Me,' verse 22, links this chapter to Isaiah 65:17 and to the vision at the close of Revelation, 21:1. The enduring name and descendants of God's people are guaranteed by the permanence of what He makes. The weekly rhythm of 'from one Sabbath to another' is the rest of Hebrews 4:9, and the gates that never close are the gates of Revelation 21:25. The book of Isaiah, which started with a rebellious nation, ends with a world gathered before its Maker, and the story of the Bible, which began in a garden, is shown on its way to a city whose light is the glory of God.

quiz.q: According to verses 1-2, whom does God say He esteems above any temple built for Him?

options.text: The one who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at His word.
The one who builds the largest and most elaborate temple.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly questions what kind of house could ever contain God.

options.text: The one who offers the most costly sacrifices regardless of heart posture.
options.note: Costly sacrifice sounds devout, but verse 3 explicitly condemns hollow sacrifice offered without right heart, likening it to violence and idolatry.

options.text: The one who avoids all forms of worship altogether.
options.note: The passage does not condemn worship itself, only worship divorced from humble, trembling hearts.

quiz.q: What is unusual about the birth described in verses 7-9?

options.text: Zion gives birth before she was even in labor, a nation delivered suddenly and miraculously.
options.note: Verses 7-8 emphasize the startling suddenness of this birth.

options.text: It describes an ordinary, lengthy childbirth with no unusual features.
options.note: The passage specifically emphasizes the birth happening before labor even began.

options.text: It describes the birth of a single individual with no national significance.
options.note: A boy is mentioned in verse 7, but the imagery is explicitly about a nation, a country born in a day, not one individual alone.

options.text: It predicts that Zion would never again bear children.
options.note: The opposite; it promises miraculous, abundant birth.

quiz.q: How does Stephen use Isaiah 66:1 in Acts 7?

options.text: He quotes it to argue that the Most High does not dwell in houses made with hands.
options.note: Acts 7:48-49 quotes this verse directly in Stephen's final sermon.

options.text: He uses it to argue that the temple should be rebuilt immediately.
options.note: Stephen's point is the opposite, that God transcends any physical temple.

options.text: He applies it only to pagan temples, not the Jerusalem temple.
options.note: This misdirects Stephen's point; he applies the broader principle that no house made with hands can contain God specifically to how the Jerusalem temple itself is regarded.

quiz.q: How does Jesus use Isaiah 66:24 in Mark 9:44-48?

options.text: He quotes it three times unchanged to describe hell, where the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.
options.note: Jesus repeats this exact language three times in Mark 9 regarding the seriousness of sin and judgment.

options.text: He quotes it to describe a temporary, minor discomfort.
options.note: Jesus uses the verse with full seriousness to describe the gravity of hell.

options.text: He rejects this Old Testament image as no longer applicable.
options.note: This is the opposite of what Jesus does; He affirms and repeats the image directly, three times, not rejecting it.

options.text: Mark's Gospel never quotes from Isaiah 66.
options.note: Mark 9:44-48 quotes this verse three times.

questions: God says He esteems the humble and contrite who tremble at His word above any grand temple or sacrifice. Is your own worship marked more by outward performance or by genuine trembling humility before God?
Zion's birth happened suddenly, before labor even began. Where in your life or church community have you seen God do something suddenly and miraculously that you had not expected or worked for?
God compares His comfort to a mother nursing and carrying her child. Is this the kind of tender, intimate comfort you actually turn to God for, or do you tend to keep Him at arm's length?
Jesus took Isaiah's closing image of unquenched fire with complete seriousness as a description of hell. Does your own view of judgment take this warning as seriously as Jesus Himself did?

The book of Isaiah, from chapter 1 to chapter 66, moves from indictment to new creation, always holding grace and warning together. As you finish this whole span of Isaiah's prophecy, what is the one truth from these last studies you most need to carry with you this week?

translationNotes.note: The groves renders a reference to sacred garden groves associated with pagan fertility worship, condemned throughout Isaiah and the broader prophetic corpus as sites of syncretistic idolatry.

Tarshish, Put, Lud, Tubal, and Javan name distant regions and peoples of the ancient world, likely Spain, parts of Africa, Asia Minor, and Greece, emphasizing the truly global scope of the nations gathered to see God's glory.
